html:
I'm an AI/ML engineer in Baltimore. I like the part of machine learning that most demos skip: what happens after the model works.

My day job is a healthcare services organization, where I built a document-intelligence pipeline that turns a flood of inbound clinical documents into structured data — custom classification and extraction models on Azure, wired through Functions, Blob Storage and Postgres — and the operational analytics platform the group reads its numbers from. I owned that pipeline's move into production, and the outage that followed it. The thing I'm proudest of there isn't a model; it's the regression workflow that makes it obvious when a number quietly changes.

Before that I fine-tuned and deployed LLMs for a production customer-service assistant, and did computer-vision research on marine sensor data at the University of Delaware's DeepREAL Lab — segmenting seafloor imagery across seventeen substrate classes. I finished an M.S. in Computer Science there in 2025, after a B.S. concentrating in AI and robotics, while rowing five seasons on the men's crew team.

Outside work I build things that are slightly too ambitious for one person: an agentic second brain, a hosting platform for agent-written apps, a creature-collection game with an AI-generated art pipeline. That's usually where I learn the most.
